claim: The glucose-sensing Mondo pathway regulates expression of metabolic genes in mammals.
source: The glucose-sensing Mondo pathway is a key regulator of energy metabolism (Abdul-Wahed et al., 2017; Richards et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Abdul-Wahed et al., 2017 and Richards et al., 2017

claim: The Mondo pathway consists of three basic helix-loop-helix/leucine zipper (bHLH/Zip) family transcription factors: MondoA, ChREBP, and Mlx.
source: It consists of three basic helix-loop-helix/leucine zipper (bHLH/Zip) family transcription factors (TFs): the two Mondo family factors 'Mlx interacting protein' (Mlxip; MondoA) and 'Mlx interacting protein-like' (Mlxipl; or ChREBP for 'carbohydrate response element binding protein') and their binding partner 'Max-like protein X' (Mlx) (Havula and Hietakangas, 2018; Richards et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Havula and Hietakangas, 2018 and Richards et al., 2017

claim: Mondo pathway factors are activated by glucose, likely via glucose-6-phosphate (G6P).
source: After their activation by glucose, likely via glucose-6-phosphate (G6P) (Dentin et al., 2012; Li et al., 2010b; Stoltzman et al., 2008), the Mondo family factors regulate gene expression as MondoA:Mlx or ChREBP:Mlx heterodimers by binding E-box type enhancer elements ('carbohydrate response elements', 'ChoREs') in the regulatory regions of their target genes (Billin et al., 2000; Jeong et al., 2011; Koo and Towle, 2000; Ma et al., 2006; Poungvarin et al., 2015; Yamashita et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dentin et al., 2012; Li et al., 2010b; Stoltzman et al., 2008

claim: Mondo family factors regulate gene expression as MondoA:Mlx or ChREBP:Mlx heterodimers by binding carbohydrate response elements (ChoREs) in regulatory regions of target genes.
source: After their activation by glucose, likely via glucose-6-phosphate (G6P) (Dentin et al., 2012; Li et al., 2010b; Stoltzman et al., 2008), the Mondo family factors regulate gene expression as MondoA:Mlx or ChREBP:Mlx heterodimers by binding E-box type enhancer elements ('carbohydrate response elements', 'ChoREs') in the regulatory regions of their target genes (Billin et al., 2000; Jeong et al., 2011; Koo and Towle, 2000; Ma et al., 2006; Poungvarin et al., 2015; Yamashita et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Billin et al., 2000; Jeong et al., 2011; Koo and Towle, 2000; Ma et al., 2006; Poungvarin et al., 2015; Yamashita et al., 2001

claim: Metabolism and metabolic signaling play a crucial role in embryonic development.
source: While recent studies have highlighted a crucial role for metabolism and metabolic signaling in embryonic development (Miyazawa and Aulehla, 2018), research on Mondo pathway function has concentrated on adult animals (Hunt et al., 2015; Iizuka et al., 2004; Imamura et al., 2014; Song et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Miyazawa and Aulehla, 2018

claim: Research on Mondo pathway function has concentrated on adult animals.
source: While recent studies have highlighted a crucial role for metabolism and metabolic signaling in embryonic development (Miyazawa and Aulehla, 2018), research on Mondo pathway function has concentrated on adult animals (Hunt et al., 2015; Iizuka et al., 2004; Imamura et al., 2014; Song et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hunt et al., 2015; Iizuka et al., 2004; Imamura et al., 2014; Song et al., 2019

claim: Zebrafish is a model for early vertebrate development.
source: As it is currently unknown if and how MondoA, ChREBP or Mlx contribute to metabolic regulation of embryogenesis, we investigated a potential developmental role of the Mondo pathway in zebrafish, a model for early vertebrate development (Nüsslein-Volhard, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nüsslein-Volhard, 2002

claim: After fertilization in zebrafish, a cap of cells (the blastoderm) forms on top of the yolk cell, which it subsequently engulfs in a morphogenetic movement called epiboly.
source: After fertilization, a cap of cells (the blastoderm) forms on top of the yolk cell, which it subsequently engulfs in a morphogenetic movement called epiboly (Bruce, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bruce, 2016

claim: Epiboly involves processes in the enveloping layer (EVL), the deep cell layer (DEL) of the blastoderm, and the yolk syncytial layer (YSL).
source: Mechanistically, epiboly involves processes both in the enveloping layer (EVL) as well as the deep cell layer (DEL) of the blastoderm and in a teleost specific structure of the yolk cell, the yolk syncytial layer (YSL).
evidence: Direct statement in the text

claim: By the end of epiboly, germ layers and body axes have been formed.
source: By the end of epiboly, germ layers and body axes have been formed.
evidence: Direct statement in the text

claim: Most developmental pathways and many facets of metabolism and its regulation are highly conserved between mammals and zebrafish.
source: Most developmental pathways as well as many facets of metabolism and its regulation are highly conserved between mammals and zebrafish (Gut et al., 2017; Schier and Talbot, 2005; Solnica-Krezel and Sepich, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gut et al., 2017; Schier and Talbot, 2005; Solnica-Krezel and Sepich, 2012

claim: Morpholino oligonucleotide (MO) mediated loss-of-function of MondoA severely impaired epiboly movements in zebrafish embryos.
source: Morpholino oligonucleotide (MO) mediated loss-of-function of MondoA severely impaired epiboly movements.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Nsdhl (NAD(P) dependent steroid dehydrogenase-like) is an enzyme involved in cholesterol biosynthesis.
source: Subsequent transcriptome analysis revealed genes deregulated upon loss of MondoA function and highlighted an enzyme involved in cholesterol biosynthesis, Nsdhl (NAD(P) dependent steroid dehydrogenase-like), as a potential key mediator of MondoA function in epiboly.
evidence: Direct statement in the text

claim: Nsdhl is a potential key mediator of MondoA function in epiboly.
source: Subsequent transcriptome analysis revealed genes deregulated upon loss of MondoA function and highlighted an enzyme involved in cholesterol biosynthesis, Nsdhl (NAD(P) dependent steroid dehydrogenase-like), as a potential key mediator of MondoA function in epiboly.
evidence: Supported by transcriptome analysis data

claim: Nsdhl-mediated cholesterol synthesis downstream of MondoA is required for the synthesis of sufficient levels of the steroid hormone pregnenolone.
source: Functional analysis of Nsdhl suggests that Nsdhl-mediated cholesterol synthesis downstream of MondoA is required for the synthesis of sufficient levels of the steroid hormone pregnenolone, which stabilizes YSL microtubules necessary for epiboly.
evidence: Supported by functional analysis data

claim: Pregnenolone stabilizes YSL microtubules necessary for epiboly.
source: Functional analysis of Nsdhl suggests that Nsdhl-mediated cholesterol synthesis downstream of MondoA is required for the synthesis of sufficient levels of the steroid hormone pregnenolone, which stabilizes YSL microtubules necessary for epiboly.
evidence: Supported by functional analysis data

claim: Maternal-zygotic (MZ) mutant embryos homozygous for a small deletion allele of mondoa showed a severe aberrant epiboly phenotype with low penetrance.
source: Maternal-zygotic (MZ) mutant embryos homozygous for a small deletion allele of mondoa leading to a premature stop codon showed a severe aberrant epiboly phenotype, albeit with low penetrance that our transcriptome analysis indicates to result from compensatory changes in the expression of cholesterol and steroid biosynthesis genes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on MZ mutants

claim: The low penetrance of the epiboly phenotype in MZ mondoa mutants results from compensatory changes in the expression of cholesterol and steroid biosynthesis genes.
source: Maternal-zygotic (MZ) mutant embryos homozygous for a small deletion allele of mondoa leading to a premature stop codon showed a severe aberrant epiboly phenotype, albeit with low penetrance that our transcriptome analysis indicates to result from compensatory changes in the expression of cholesterol and steroid biosynthesis genes.
evidence: Supported by transcriptome analysis data

claim: One single orthologue of each Mondo pathway member (MondoA, ChREBP, and Mlx) is present in the zebrafish genome.
source: For each of the Mondo pathway members MondoA, ChREBP and Mlx one single orthologue is present in the zebrafish genome (GRCz11/danRer11).
evidence: Direct statement based on genome analysis

claim: Zebrafish mondoa, chrebp and mlx cluster with their mammalian and chicken homologs in phylogenetic analysis.
source: Phylogenetic analysis showed that zebrafish mondoa, chrebp and mlx cluster with their mammalian and chicken homologs (Figure 1A) and revealed a high level of protein sequence conservation between zebrafish and human orthologs (Figure 1B), especially of the glucose-sensing module (GSM) specific to the Mondo family and of the DNA binding bHLH/Zip domains.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: There is a high level of protein sequence conservation between zebrafish and human orthologs of Mondo pathway members, especially of the glucose-sensing module (GSM) and the DNA binding bHLH/Zip domains.
source: Phylogenetic analysis showed that zebrafish mondoa, chrebp and mlx cluster with their mammalian and chicken homologs (Figure 1A) and revealed a high level of protein sequence conservation between zebrafish and human orthologs (Figure 1B), especially of the glucose-sensing module (GSM) specific to the Mondo family and of the DNA binding bHLH/Zip domains.
evidence: Supported by sequence conservation analysis shown in Figure 1B

claim: The high level of protein sequence conservation between zebrafish and human Mondo pathway orthologs suggests that the functions of these proteins are conserved.
source: This finding suggests that the functions of these proteins are conserved.
evidence: Inference based on sequence conservation data

claim: All three Mondo pathway factors (mondoa, chrebp, mlx) are expressed in PAC2 cells.
source: All three Mondo pathway factors are expressed in these cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: The 2xChoRE reporter construct was active in HepG2 cells.
source: This construct was active in HepG2 cells, a mammalian cell culture model commonly used for Mondo pathway studies (Kim et al., 1996; Yu and Luo, 2009; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: In PAC2 cells, bioluminescence from the 2xChoRE reporter increased in a dose-dependent manner upon glucose treatment.
source: In PAC2 cells, bioluminescence equally increased in a dose-dependent manner upon glucose treatment (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 1C

claim: No significant changes in bioluminescence levels were detected upon glucose treatment in PAC2 cells expressing a constitutively active luciferase reporter (pGL3-Control).
source: No significant changes in bioluminescence levels were detected upon glucose treatment in cells expressing a constitutively active luciferase reporter (pGL3-Control; Figure 1D), excluding a general unspecific increase in transcriptional activity by glucose treatment.
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Transient overexpression of MondoA and Mlx activated transcription from the 2xChoRE reporter under low glucose conditions in PAC2 cells.
source: Transient overexpression of MondoA and Mlx activated transcription from the reporter also under low glucose conditions (Figure 1E), as shown by the increased bioluminescence compared with transfection of the 2xChoRE reporter alone (p≤0.001).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 1E

claim: Overexpression of MondoA and Mlx together led to a more pronounced effect on bioluminescence than overexpression of either factor alone, revealing synergistic effects.
source: Overexpression of the MondoA and Mlx factors together led to an even more pronounced effect on bioluminescence (p≤0.01), revealing synergistic effects.
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 1E

claim: High glucose levels caused significant reporter gene induction in control PAC2 cells.
source: High glucose levels caused significant reporter gene induction in control cells (p≤0.01; Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 1E

claim: Strong glucose induction of the 2xChoRE reporter was shown by PAC2 cells overexpressing either Mlx or MondoA alone as well as both factors together.
source: Importantly, strong glucose induction of the reporter was also shown by cells overexpressing either Mlx (p≤0.01) or MondoA (p≤0.001) alone as well as both factors together (p≤0.001; Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 1E

claim: An unrelated control reporter construct (pGRE-Luc) was not responsive to glucose or Mondo pathway factor overexpression treatments.
source: An unrelated control reporter construct (pGRE-Luc, Weger et al., 2012) was not responsive to any of the treatments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: Limited availability of endogenous Mondo pathway components restrains pathway activity in PAC2 cells.
source: Together, the data indicate that limited availability of endogenous pathway components restrains pathway activity, and that both basal activity and the response to higher glucose levels are potentiated when more sensor proteins are available.
evidence: Inference based on overexpression data

claim: Both basal activity and the response to higher glucose levels of the Mondo pathway are potentiated when more sensor proteins are available.
source: Together, the data indicate that limited availability of endogenous pathway components restrains pathway activity, and that both basal activity and the response to higher glucose levels are potentiated when more sensor proteins are available.
evidence: Inference based on overexpression data

claim: PAC2 cells transfected with a control 5 bp mismatch MO (mondoa-mis) showed a 2.0-fold induction of bioluminescence from the 2xChoRE reporter by high glucose levels.
source: Cells transfected with a control 5 bp mismatch MO (mondoa-mis) showed a 2.0-fold induction of bioluminescence from the 2xChoRE reporter plasmid by high glucose levels, while in cells transfected with a MO directed against the translation start site (mondoa-mo) this glucose response was abolished (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 1F

claim: In PAC2 cells transfected with mondoa-mo, the glucose response of the 2xChoRE reporter was abolished.
source: Cells transfected with a control 5 bp mismatch MO (mondoa-mis) showed a 2.0-fold induction of bioluminescence from the 2xChoRE reporter plasmid by high glucose levels, while in cells transfected with a MO directed against the translation start site (mondoa-mo) this glucose response was abolished (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 1F

claim: ChoRE mediated glucose induction of gene expression is regulated by the Mondo pathway in zebrafish.
source: Taken together, our data demonstrate that ChoRE mediated glucose induction of gene expression is regulated by the Mondo pathway also in zebrafish.
evidence: Conclusion based on multiple experimental results in PAC2 cells

claim: Maternal transcripts of mondoa, chrebp and mlx are present in zebrafish embryos.
source: We reanalyzed a previously published zebrafish developmental transcriptome dataset (White et al., 2017, ENA accession number ERP014517) and detected maternal transcripts of mondoa, chrebp and mlx as well as expression of the three genes throughout development, following distinct temporal patterns (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: Supported by transcriptome data shown in Figure 1G-I

claim: mondoa, chrebp and mlx are expressed throughout zebrafish development, following distinct temporal patterns.
source: We reanalyzed a previously published zebrafish developmental transcriptome dataset (White et al., 2017, ENA accession number ERP014517) and detected maternal transcripts of mondoa, chrebp and mlx as well as expression of the three genes throughout development, following distinct temporal patterns (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: Supported by transcriptome data shown in Figure 1G-I

claim: mondoa shows a ubiquitous expression pattern in zebrafish embryos.
source: Whole mount in situ hybridization analysis (WISH) for mondoa revealed a ubiquitous expression pattern (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by WISH data shown in Figure 1J

claim: chrebp and mlx show ubiquitous expression patterns in zebrafish embryos.
source: Similar results were observed for chrebp and mlx (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by WISH data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E

claim: At the 50% epiboly stage, mondoa, chrebp and mlx are expressed throughout the zebrafish embryo.
source: At the 50% epiboly stage, all three genes are expressed throughout the embryo (Figure 1K; Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by WISH data shown in Figure 1K and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F

claim: Glucose treatment significantly increased expression of hk2 in early zebrafish embryos.
source: This treatment significantly increased expression of hk2 (p<0.001), fasn (p<0.01) and txnipa (p<0.001; Figure 1L–N), but not of the control gene eef1a1l1/ef1a (eukaryotic translation elongation factor 1 alpha 1 (Figure 1O), ruling out a nonspecific general increase in gene expression by 2-DG treatment.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1L

claim: Glucose treatment significantly increased expression of fasn in early zebrafish embryos.
source: This treatment significantly increased expression of hk2 (p<0.001), fasn (p<0.01) and txnipa (p<0.001; Figure 1L–N), but not of the control gene eef1a1l1/ef1a (eukaryotic translation elongation factor 1 alpha 1 (Figure 1O), ruling out a nonspecific general increase in gene expression by 2-DG treatment.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1M

claim: Glucose treatment significantly increased expression of txnipa in early zebrafish embryos.
source: This treatment significantly increased expression of hk2 (p<0.001), fasn (p<0.01) and txnipa (p<0.001; Figure 1L–N), but not of the control gene eef1a1l1/ef1a (eukaryotic translation elongation factor 1 alpha 1 (Figure 1O), ruling out a nonspecific general increase in gene expression by 2-DG treatment.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1N

claim: Glucose treatment did not increase expression of the control gene eef1a1l1/ef1a in early zebrafish embryos.
source: This treatment significantly increased expression of hk2 (p<0.001), fasn (p<0.01) and txnipa (p<0.001; Figure 1L–N), but not of the control gene eef1a1l1/ef1a (eukaryotic translation elongation factor 1 alpha 1 (Figure 1O), ruling out a nonspecific general increase in gene expression by 2-DG treatment.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1O

claim: txnipa expression was not induced by 2-DG in embryos injected with mondoa-mo.
source: Furthermore, txnipa expression was not induced by 2-DG in embryos injected with mondoa-mo, showing that MondoA function is required for its induction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G

claim: MondoA function is required for 2-DG induction of txnipa expression in zebrafish embryos.
source: Furthermore, txnipa expression was not induced by 2-DG in embryos injected with mondoa-mo, showing that MondoA function is required for its induction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G

claim: Embryos treated with 2-DG showed a 2.3-fold increase in bioluminescence from the 2xChoRE luciferase reporter over the control.
source: Embryos treated with 2-DG (n = 72) showed a 2.3-fold increase (p≤0.01) in bioluminescence over the control (n = 78; Figure 1P).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 1P

claim: Mondo pathway mediated glucose signaling is present in zebrafish embryos as early as at the sphere stage.
source: Together, these results suggest that Mondo pathway mediated glucose signaling is present in embryos as early as at the sphere stage.
evidence: Conclusion based on multiple experimental results in embryos

claim: Injections of a MO directed against chrebp did not result in an aberrant phenotype in zebrafish embryos.
source: While injections of a MO directed against chrebp did not result in an aberrant phenotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B), mondoa-mo injected embryos showed a striking delay in epiboly movements when compared with uninjected or mondoa-mis injected embryos (Figure 2A–D; Video 1).
evidence: Supported by phenotype data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: mondoa-mo injected embryos showed a striking delay in epiboly movements when compared with uninjected or mondoa-mis injected embryos.
source: While injections of a MO directed against chrebp did not result in an aberrant phenotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B), mondoa-mo injected embryos showed a striking delay in epiboly movements when compared with uninjected or mondoa-mis injected embryos (Figure 2A–D; Video 1).
evidence: Supported by phenotype data shown in Figure 2A-D and Video 1

claim: The epiboly delay phenotype in mondoa morphants was dose-dependent, with the strongest delay occurring at the highest concentration.
source: This phenotype was dose-dependent, with the strongest delay occurring at the highest concentration (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by phenotype data shown in Figure 2A

claim: GFP expression from a reporter construct carrying the mondoa target sequence was efficiently abolished by co-injection of mondoa-mo, but not mondoa-mis.
source: GFP expression from a reporter construct carrying the target sequence was efficiently abolished by co-injection of mondoa-mo, but not mondoa-mis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by GFP expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C

claim: Co-injection of mondoa-mo and p53-mo led to the same phenotype as observed upon injection with mondoa-mo alone.
source: An involvement of P53-mediated apoptosis in the observed phenotypes was ruled out by co-injection of mondoa-mo and a MO directed against p53 (p53-mo), leading to the same phenotype as observed upon injection with mondoa-mo alone (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by phenotype data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: P53-mediated apoptosis is not involved in the epiboly phenotype observed in mondoa morphants.
source: An involvement of P53-mediated apoptosis in the observed phenotypes was ruled out by co-injection of mondoa-mo and a MO directed against p53 (p53-mo), leading to the same phenotype as observed upon injection with mondoa-mo alone (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by phenotype data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: Knockdown of mlx with mlx-mo showed a dose-dependent impairment of epiboly similar to the one observed with mondoa-mo, albeit somewhat less severe.
source: Knockdown of the mondoa cofactor mlx with a MO directed against the translation start site of mlx (mlx-mo) showed a dose-dependent impairment of epiboly similar to the one observed with mondoa-mo, albeit somewhat less severe (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Supported by phenotype data shown in Figure 2C,D

claim: MondoA forms heterodimers with Mlx to exert its function in epiboly.
source: These results are consistent with the model that MondoA forms heterodimers with Mlx to exert its function also in epiboly.
evidence: Inference based on mlx knockdown phenotype

claim: Embryos injected with only mondoa-mo reached 38% epiboly, whereas embryos co-injected with mondoa mRNA arrived at 47% epiboly.
source: Embryos injected with only mondoa-mo reached 38% epiboly, whereas embryos co-injected with mondoa mRNA arrived at 47% epiboly (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by epiboly progression data shown in Figure 2E

claim: mondoa-mo specifically targets mondoa gene function.
source: In conclusion, these observations indicate that mondoa-mo specifically targets mondoa gene function, and reveal that loss of MondoA function severely impacts on epiboly during zebrafish development.
evidence: Conclusion based on multiple control experiments

claim: Loss of MondoA function severely impacts on epiboly during zebrafish development.
source: In conclusion, these observations indicate that mondoa-mo specifically targets mondoa gene function, and reveal that loss of MondoA function severely impacts on epiboly during zebrafish development.
evidence: Conclusion based on multiple experimental results

claim: Energy charge was unaltered in mondoa morphants.
source: Our results showed that energy charge was unaltered in the morphants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by energy charge data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: mondoa morphants had similar numbers of cells as control embryos.
source: As shown by this analysis, mondoa morphants had similar numbers of cells as control embryos (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Cell density was higher in mondoa morphants compared to mismatch controls.
source: Accordingly, the cell density was higher in mondoa morphants compared to mismatch controls, as movement to the vegetal pole was impaired while cells continued to divide (Figure 3B,C; Videos 2–4).
evidence: Supported by cell density data shown in Figure 3B,C and Videos 2-4

claim: Germ ring-like thickenings were observed in mondoa morphants.
source: In addition, we observed germ ring-like thickenings (Figure 2A,C; arrowheads) as well as internalization of cells at the blastoderm margin in mondoa morphants (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D; Videos 5 and 6).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2A,C

claim: Internalization of cells at the blastoderm margin was observed in mondoa morphants.
source: In addition, we observed germ ring-like thickenings (Figure 2A,C; arrowheads) as well as internalization of cells at the blastoderm margin in mondoa morphants (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D; Videos 5 and 6).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D and Videos 5 and 6

claim: The average migration speed of deep cells was identical for mondoa morphants and controls.
source: Furthermore, the average migration speed of deep cells was identical for morphants and controls, demonstrating normal individual cell migration capacity in morphants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by cell migration speed data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E

claim: mondoa morphants have normal individual cell migration capacity.
source: Furthermore, the average migration speed of deep cells was identical for morphants and controls, demonstrating normal individual cell migration capacity in morphants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by cell migration speed data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E

claim: EVL cells continued to progress and could reach a position vegetally to the YSL nuclei in mondoa morphants.
source: Our observations revealed that EVL cells continued to progress and could reach a position vegetally to the YSL nuclei in the morphants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–F, Video 7).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-F and Video 7

claim: EVL integrity was intact in mondoa morphants.
source: Consistently, EVL integrity as revealed by rhodamine-phalloidin staining (Lepage and Bruce, 2010; Lepage et al., 2014) was intact in the morphants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: Supported by phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G-H

claim: EVL epiboly still occurs in mondoa morphants.
source: These findings indicate that EVL epiboly still occurs in the morphants.
evidence: Inference based on EVL cell progression and integrity data

claim: Deep cells of mondoa morphants lagged behind both EVL and YSL layers.
source: However, deep cells of mondoa morphants lagged behind both EVL and YSL layers, consistent with models suggesting rather passive movement of these cells into spaces left open by the other two layers (Bensch et al., 2013; Song et al., 2013; Figure 4A,B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-F

claim: In mondoa morphants, a few deep cells were detected more vegetally than the YSL nuclei.
source: Nevertheless, in mondoa morphants a few deep cells were detected more vegetally than the YSL nuclei.
evidence: Observation from imaging data

claim: YSL nuclei showed a much broader and more disorganized distribution in mondoa morphants than in control injected or wild-type embryos.
source: Also, YSL nuclei showed a much broader and more disorganized distribution than in control injected or wild-type embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-F

claim: YSL nuclei appeared to cluster and to break away from the blastoderm margin in mondoa morphants.
source: YSL nuclei appeared to cluster and to break away from the blastoderm margin (Figure 4B, white arrow), in contrast to the more even distribution in a relatively narrow band around the margin in wild-type embryos.
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B

claim: A defect in YSL structure or function is a potential reason for the impaired epiboly in mondoa morphants.
source: These findings pointed to a defect in YSL structure or function as a potential reason for the impaired epiboly in mondoa morphants.
evidence: Inference based on YSL abnormalities observed

claim: mondoa knockdown limited to the YSL led to epiboly delay and developmental arrest compared with uninjected or control injected embryos.
source: Strikingly, mondoa knockdown limited to the YSL still led to epiboly delay and developmental arrest compared with uninjected or control injected embryos (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by phenotype data shown in Figure 4D

claim: No major perturbations of marginal endocytosis were found in mondoa morphants.
source: However, we did not find any evidence for major perturbations of marginal endocytosis or blastoderm patterning in the morphants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J–Q).
evidence: Supported by endocytosis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1J-Q

claim: No major perturbations of blastoderm patterning were found in mondoa morphants.
source: However, we did not find any evidence for major perturbations of marginal endocytosis or blastoderm patterning in the morphants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J–Q).
evidence: Supported by patterning data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1J-Q

claim: nsdhl was the gene most down-regulated by mondoa-knockdown.
source: Interestingly, the gene most down-regulated by mondoa-knockdown was nsdhl (NAD(P) dependent steroid dehydrogenase-like; Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Nsdhl catalyzes steps in the conversion of the cholesterol precursor lanosterol to zymosterol.
source: Nsdhl is part of the cholesterol biogenesis pathway, catalyzing steps in the conversion of the cholesterol precursor lanosterol to zymosterol (Figure 5B).
evidence: Direct statement based on known biochemical function

claim: Both the 'sterol biosynthesis' pathway and the upstream 'terpenoid backbone biosynthesis' pathway are coordinately downregulated in mondoa morphants.
source: Consistently, a global metabolic pathway gene set enrichment analysis revealed that both the 'sterol biosynthesis' pathway, of which Nsdhl is part, and the upstream 'terpenoid backbone biosynthesis' pathway are coordinately downregulated in the morphants (Supplementary file 2, Figure 5B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data shown in Supplementary file 2, Figure 5B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: A significant increase of basal nsdhl transcript levels was observed upon 2-DG injection in early embryos.
source: We observed a significant increase of basal nsdhl transcript levels upon 2-DG injection (p≤0.05) and upon overexpression of both MondoA and Mlx (p≤0.001) in early embryos, which was augmented further when both treatments were combined (p≤0.001; Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5C

claim: A significant increase of basal nsdhl transcript levels was observed upon overexpression of both MondoA and Mlx in early embryos.
source: We observed a significant increase of basal nsdhl transcript levels upon 2-DG injection (p≤0.05) and upon overexpression of both MondoA and Mlx (p≤0.001) in early embryos, which was augmented further when both treatments were combined (p≤0.001; Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5C

claim: The increase in nsdhl transcript levels was augmented further when 2-DG injection and MondoA/Mlx overexpression were combined.
source: We observed a significant increase of basal nsdhl transcript levels upon 2-DG injection (p≤0.05) and upon overexpression of both MondoA and Mlx (p≤0.001) in early embryos, which was augmented further when both treatments were combined (p≤0.001; Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5C

claim: No changes in ef1a expression were observed under 2-DG injection or MondoA/Mlx overexpression conditions.
source: No changes in expression were observed for ef1a under these conditions (Figure 5D), confirming the target gene specific effects of the treatments.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5D

claim: The Mondo pathway mediates glucose regulation of nsdhl expression.
source: Together, these results strongly suggest that the Mondo pathway mediates glucose regulation of nsdhl expression, thereby linking glucose sensing with cholesterol synthesis.
evidence: Conclusion based on nsdhl expression data

claim: The Mondo pathway links glucose sensing with cholesterol synthesis.
source: Together, these results strongly suggest that the Mondo pathway mediates glucose regulation of nsdhl expression, thereby linking glucose sensing with cholesterol synthesis.
evidence: Conclusion based on nsdhl expression data

claim: nsdhl-mo injected embryos arrested at 50% epiboly when control embryos had completed epiboly.
source: We observed a highly similar phenotype to the mondoa knockdown phenotype, with nsdhl-mo injected embryos arrested at 50% epiboly when control embryos had completed epiboly (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: Supported by phenotype data shown in Figure 5E,F

claim: nsdhl is ubiquitously expressed in the zebrafish embryo, including the YSL.
source: As mondoa, nsdhl is ubiquitously expressed in the embryo, including the YSL (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F,G), and injection of nsdhl-mo into the yolk cell at the 1 k-cell stage resulted in an epiboly delay and developmental arrest as observed for YSL specific mondoa knockdown (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by WISH data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F,G

claim: Injection of nsdhl-mo into the yolk cell at the 1 k-cell stage resulted in an epiboly delay and developmental arrest.
source: As mondoa, nsdhl is ubiquitously expressed in the embryo, including the YSL (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F,G), and injection of nsdhl-mo into the yolk cell at the 1 k-cell stage resulted in an epiboly delay and developmental arrest as observed for YSL specific mondoa knockdown (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by phenotype data shown in Figure 5G

claim: The function of Nsdhl in the biosynthesis pathway to cholesterol in the YSL is essential for epiboly movements.
source: Thus, the function of Nsdhl in the biosynthesis pathway to cholesterol in the YSL appears to be essential for epiboly movements.
evidence: Conclusion based on YSL-specific nsdhl knockdown data

claim: Treatment with pregnenolone partially rescued epiboly in mondoa-mo injected embryos.
source: Treatment with pregnenolone indeed partially rescued epiboly in mondoa-mo injected embryos (Figure 5H) at a level comparable to the rescue with mondoa mRNA.
evidence: Supported by epiboly progression data shown in Figure 5H

claim: The aberrant epiboly phenotype of nsdhl morphants was partially rescued by pregnenolone treatment.
source: Accordingly, the aberrant epiboly phenotype of nsdhl morphants was also partially rescued by pregnenolone treatment (Figure 5I), confirming its role downstream of the MondoA/Nsdhl pathway.
evidence: Supported by epiboly progression data shown in Figure 5I

claim: Pregnenolone functions downstream of the MondoA/Nsdhl pathway.
source: Accordingly, the aberrant epiboly phenotype of nsdhl morphants was also partially rescued by pregnenolone treatment (Figure 5I), confirming its role downstream of the MondoA/Nsdhl pathway.
evidence: Supported by rescue data shown in Figure 5I

claim: Pregnenolone regulates epiboly by mediating microtubule stability.
source: Pregnenolone was shown to regulate epiboly by mediating microtubule stability (Hsu et al., 2006; Schwend et al., 2011; Weng et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hsu et al., 2006; Schwend et al., 2011; Weng et al., 2013

claim: In uninjected embryos, the YSL forms a regular band below the blastoderm, with yolk syncytial layer nuclei (YSN) surrounded by microtubule organizing centers (MTOCs).
source: In uninjected embryos (n = 9/9), the YSL forms a regular band below the blastoderm, with yolk syncytial layer nuclei (YSN) surrounded by microtubule organizing centers (MTOCs) (Solnica-Krezel and Driever, 1994; Strähle and Jesuthasan, 1993; Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A and citations to Solnica-Krezel and Driever, 1994; Strähle and Jesuthasan, 1993

claim: Dense arrays of microtubules spread from the MTOCs along the animal-vegetal axis into the yolk cytoplasmic layer (YCL), forming root-like bundles in uninjected embryos.
source: Below this area, dense arrays of microtubules spread from the MTOCs along the animal-vegetal axis into the yolk cytoplasmic layer (YCL), forming root-like bundles.
evidence: Observation from imaging data

claim: mondoa-mo injected embryos showed a rather unstructured YSL with a less well defined border compared with control embryos.
source: Compared with the control embryos (Figure 6C,D), mondoa-mo injected embryos showed a rather unstructured YSL with a less well defined border (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6C-F

claim: YSN were less regularly arranged in mondoa-mo injected embryos, and their associated MTOCs formed stellar structures.
source: YSN were less regularly arranged, and their associated MTOCs formed stellar structures (n = 14/16; Figure 6B), apparently reflecting shortened microtubules that did not form the arrays of root-like bundles along the animal-vegetal axis seen in uninjected controls.
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The stellar structures formed by MTOCs in mondoa morphants reflect shortened microtubules that did not form the arrays of root-like bundles along the animal-vegetal axis seen in uninjected controls.
source: YSN were less regularly arranged, and their associated MTOCs formed stellar structures (n = 14/16; Figure 6B), apparently reflecting shortened microtubules that did not form the arrays of root-like bundles along the animal-vegetal axis seen in uninjected controls.
evidence: Inference based on imaging data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The YSL of mondoa morphants treated with pregnenolone appeared to be better organized compared to the untreated morphants.
source: Importantly, the YSL of morphants treated with pregnenolone appeared to be better organized compared to the untreated morphants because the YSN and their corresponding MTOCs were arranged as in the uninjected control (n = 6/9; Figure 6B,G,H).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6B,G,H

claim: In pregnenolone treated mondoa morphants, the microtubule arrays were longer and formed array-like structures along the animal-vegetal axis of the embryos similar to the control.
source: Furthermore, in pregnenolone treated embryos, the microtubule arrays were longer and formed array-like structures along the animal-vegetal axis of the embryos similar to the control.
evidence: Observation from imaging data

claim: MondoA functions in epiboly via the stabilization of yolk microtubules by pregnenolone formed downstream of cholesterol biosynthesis.
source: Taken together, these results strongly suggest that MondoA functions in epiboly via the stabilization of yolk microtubules by pregnenolone formed downstream of cholesterol biosynthesis.
evidence: Conclusion based on microtubule staining and pregnenolone rescue data

claim: A mutant allele of mondoa carried a 5 bp deletion in exon 3, leading to a frameshift in the coding sequence and a predicted premature stop eliminating both the DNA binding domain and most of the glucose-sensing domain.
source: We identified a mutant allele transmitted through the germline that carried a 5 bp deletion in exon 3 (Figure 7A), leading to a frameshift in the coding sequence and a predicted premature stop eliminating both the DNA binding domain and most of the glucose-sensing domain.
evidence: Supported by genetic analysis data shown in Figure 7A

claim: Embryos homozygous for the mondoa mutant allele did not show an aberrant embryonic phenotype and were raised to sexual maturity.
source: Embryos homozygous for this allele did not show an aberrant embryonic phenotype and were raised to sexual maturity (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: Supported by phenotype data shown in Figure 7B,C

claim: A few maternal-zygotic (MZ) mutants from incrosses of homozygous mutant parents showed a severe epiboly delay and an arrest in mid-epiboly.
source: By contrast, we found a few maternal-zygotic (MZ) mutants from incrosses of homozygous mutant parents that showed a severe epiboly delay and an arrest in mid-epiboly (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: Supported by phenotype data shown in Figure 7B,C

claim: On average 5.09 ± 1.25% of MZmondoa mutants showed an aberrant epiboly phenotype compared to 0.10 ± 0.07% in wild-type and 0.71 ± 0.39% in Zmondoa mutant embryos.
source: On average 5.09 ± 1.25% of MZmondoa mutants (n = 249/5119 embryos) showed an aberrant epiboly phenotype compared to 0.10 ± 0.07% in wild-type (WT; n = 1/1016 embryos) and 0.71 ± 0.39% in Zmondoa mutant embryos (n = 3/549 embryos).
evidence: Supported by phenotype quantification data

claim: MZmondoa mutants exhibited resistance to epiboly perturbance caused by mondoa-mo.
source: MZmondoa mutants exhibited resistance to epiboly perturbance caused by mondoa-mo, confirming specificity of the morphant phenotype (n = 3, ≥18 embryos/replicate and condition, treatment/genotype combinations blinded for analysis).
evidence: Supported by experimental data on MO injection into mutants

claim: The resistance of MZmondoa mutants to mondoa-mo confirms specificity of the morphant phenotype.
source: MZmondoa mutants exhibited resistance to epiboly perturbance caused by mondoa-mo, confirming specificity of the morphant phenotype (n = 3, ≥18 embryos/replicate and condition, treatment/genotype combinations blinded for analysis).
evidence: Inference based on resistance data

claim: The low penetrance of the epiboly phenotype in the MZ mutants is indicative of compensatory mechanisms that counteract the loss of function of mondoa.
source: The low penetrance of the epiboly phenotype in the MZ mutants is indicative of compensatory mechanisms that counteract the loss of function of mondoa.
evidence: Inference based on low penetrance observation

claim: The resistance of MZmondoa mutants to mondoa-mo strongly suggests the presence of strong compensatory or buffering mechanisms that enable embryonic development even when MondoA function is genetically perturbed.
source: Indeed, we observed a resistance of the mutants to the perturbance of epiboly caused by this MO in wild-types (Figure 7D). This observation strongly suggests the presence of strong compensatory or buffering mechanisms that enable embryonic development even when MondoA function is genetically perturbed.
evidence: Inference based on resistance data shown in Figure 7D

claim: Neither chrebp nor mlx were significantly upregulated in MZmondoa mutants.
source: Neither chrebp, the paralogue of mondoa, nor the MondoA partner mlx were significantly upregulated in MZmondoa mutants, even though trends (p=0.06) for elevated mRNA levels were seen for mlx in both mutant phenotypes and for chrebp in the affected phenotype only (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7E

claim: nsdhl gene expression was comparable to wild-type embryos in both MZmondoa mutant phenotypes (affected and unaffected epiboly).
source: Our analysis showed that nsdhl gene expression was comparable to wild-type embryos in both MZmondoa mutant phenotypes (affected and unaffected epiboly) and, thus, was compensated in both (Supplementary file 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 2E–F).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Supplementary file 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 2E-F

claim: The restoration of nsdhl expression to wild-type levels by itself was not sufficient for compensation of the epiboly phenotype in MZmondoa mutants.
source: Therefore, differences in nsdhl expression between MZmondoa mutants cannot explain the differences in the epiboly phenotype. This observation indicates that the restoration of expression to wild-type levels of this most downregulated gene upon mondoa knockdown by itself was not sufficient for compensation.
evidence: Inference based on nsdhl expression data

claim: In both MZmondoa mutant phenotypes, the entire sterol biosynthesis pathway lacked the coordinated downregulation that was seen in the morphants.
source: Consistently, in both mutant phenotypes the entire sterol biosynthesis pathway of which nsdhl forms part (Figure 5B) lacked the coordinated downregulation that was seen in the morphants (unaffected: p=0.87, affected: p=0.79; Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A

claim: mondoa morphants showed a significant downregulation in terpenoid backbone biosynthesis and sterol biosynthesis pathways.
source: mondoa morphants showed a significant downregulation in terpenoid backbone biosynthesis (p=0.016) as well as in sterol biosynthesis pathways (p=0.022; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data shown in Supplementary file 2

claim: MZmondoa mutants with unaffected epiboly showed a coordinated upregulation of terpenoid pathway genes.
source: By contrast, MZmondoa mutants with unaffected epiboly showed a coordinated upregulation of terpenoid pathway genes (i.e., they showed a statistically significant enrichment for upregulation in a directional gene set enrichment test; p=0.012; Figure 7F–G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 7F-G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 2

claim: MZmondoa mutants with affected epiboly lacked the significant coordinated upregulation in the terpenoid backbone biosynthesis pathway that was present in unaffected mutants.
source: Intriguingly, mutants with affected epiboly lacked this significant coordinated upregulation in the terpenoid backbone biosynthesis pathway that was present in unaffected mutants (p=0.178; Figure 7F–G and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 7F-G and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B

claim: The upregulation of gene expression in the terpenoid backbone biosynthesis pathway is a compensation response specifically required to restore the normal epiboly phenotype in MZmondoa mutants.
source: This key difference highlights the upregulation of gene expression in the terpenoid backbone biosynthesis pathway as a compensation response specifically required to restore the normal epiboly phenotype.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of affected and unaffected mutants

claim: Gene expression of steroid hormone biosynthesis pathway genes showed a coordinated upregulation in MZmondoa mutants with unaffected epiboly.
source: We additionally observed that gene expression of steroid hormone biosynthesis pathway genes showed a coordinated upregulation in MZmondoa mutants with unaffected epiboly (p=0.033; Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), probably to compensate for reduced flux through the biosynthesis pathways upstream.
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C

claim: The coordinated upregulation of steroid hormone biosynthesis pathway genes in MZmondoa mutants with unaffected epiboly is probably to compensate for reduced flux through the biosynthesis pathways upstream.
source: We additionally observed that gene expression of steroid hormone biosynthesis pathway genes showed a coordinated upregulation in MZmondoa mutants with unaffected epiboly (p=0.033; Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), probably to compensate for reduced flux through the biosynthesis pathways upstream.
evidence: Inference based on gene expression data

claim: MZmondoa mutants with aberrant epiboly phenotype also showed coordinated upregulation of steroid hormone biosynthesis pathway genes.
source: This upregulation was also shown by MZmondoa mutants with aberrant epiboly phenotype (p=0.017; Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C

claim: The upregulation of steroid hormone biosynthesis pathway genes was increased in MZmondoa mutants with aberrant epiboly phenotype when compared to the mutants with unaffected epiboly.
source: Strikingly, it was even increased when compared to the mutants with unaffected epiboly (p=0.049), and thereby led to strongly increased expression levels compared to wild-type.
evidence: Supported by gene expression comparison data

claim: In the absence of coordinated regulation of genes in the terpenoid pathway, the upregulation of steroid hormone biosynthesis genes was not sufficient to rescue epiboly progression in MZmondoa mutants with affected epiboly.
source: However, in the absence of coordinated regulation of genes in the terpenoid pathway, this regulation was apparently not sufficient to rescue epiboly progression.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of affected and unaffected mutants

claim: MZmondoa mutants with affected epiboly fail to properly regulate the entire set of genes necessary for epiboly progression.
source: Taken together, despite some successful compensatory gene expression regulations, MZmondoa mutants with affected epiboly fail to properly regulate the entire set of genes necessary for epiboly progression.
evidence: Conclusion based on gene expression analysis

claim: MZmondoa mutants with affected epiboly are not lacking compensation per se, but their compensation is inadequate and fails.
source: They are not lacking compensation per se, but their compensation is inadequate and fails.
evidence: Conclusion based on gene expression analysis

claim: Results from both MO mediated and genetic loss-of-function of MondoA revealed MondoA as a key developmental regulator of progression through epiboly.
source: In summary, results from both MO mediated and genetic loss-of-function of MondoA revealed MondoA as a key developmental regulator of progression through epiboly by regulating expression of cholesterol/steroidogenesis pathway genes important for yolk cell microtubule function.
evidence: Conclusion based on all experimental results

claim: MondoA regulates progression through epiboly by regulating expression of cholesterol/steroidogenesis pathway genes important for yolk cell microtubule function.
source: In summary, results from both MO mediated and genetic loss-of-function of MondoA revealed MondoA as a key developmental regulator of progression through epiboly by regulating expression of cholesterol/steroidogenesis pathway genes important for yolk cell microtubule function.
evidence: Conclusion based on all experimental results

claim: This study is the first to demonstrate conserved Mondo signaling mechanisms between zebrafish and mammals.
source: To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first study demonstrating conserved Mondo signaling mechanisms between zebrafish and mammals and linking its function to early embryonic development of vertebrates.
evidence: Statement of novelty by authors

claim: This study is the first to link Mondo pathway function to early embryonic development of vertebrates.
source: To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first study demonstrating conserved Mondo signaling mechanisms between zebrafish and mammals and linking its function to early embryonic development of vertebrates.
evidence: Statement of novelty by authors

claim: Loss of function of the Mlx orthologue in Drosophila is lethal at the late pupal stage.
source: Loss of function of the Mlx orthologue in Drosophila is lethal at the late pupal stage (Havula et al., 2013), while knockdown of a distant Mlx homolog in C. elegans affected movements of ray one precursor cells (Pickett et al., 2007), which will form a subset of male-specific sense organs in the tail.
evidence: Supported by citation to Havula et al., 2013

claim: Knockdown of a distant Mlx homolog in C. elegans affected movements of ray one precursor cells.
source: Loss of function of the Mlx orthologue in Drosophila is lethal at the late pupal stage (Havula et al., 2013), while knockdown of a distant Mlx homolog in C. elegans affected movements of ray one precursor cells (Pickett et al., 2007), which will form a subset of male-specific sense organs in the tail.
evidence: Supported by citation to Pickett et al., 2007

claim: The role of MondoA in cholesterol/steroid metabolism uncovered in zebrafish may be a feature conserved across vertebrates.
source: It is tempting to speculate that the role of MondoA in cholesterol/steroid metabolism we here uncover in the zebrafish is a feature conserved across vertebrates, albeit not much is known in mammals.
evidence: Speculation based on study findings

claim: 'Sterol biosynthetic process' is one category of genes upregulated in MondoA deficient HeLa cells under conditions of acidosis.
source: One in vitro study described 'sterol biosynthetic process' as one category of genes upregulated in MondoA deficient HeLa cells under conditions of acidosis (Wilde et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wilde et al., 2019

claim: 'Cholesterol biosynthesis' genes are upregulated in the liver of Chrebp knockout mice which were fed with a high fructose diet.
source: For the MondoA paralogue Chrebp, a study in vivo reported that 'cholesterol biosynthesis' genes are upregulated in the liver of Chrebp knockout mice which were fed with a high fructose diet (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2017

claim: The Mondo pathway plays an important role in the regulation of cholesterol/steroid metabolism under non-disease conditions.
source: While these studies were performed under specific disease conditions (i.e., a human cancer cell line under acidosis conditions or animals fed with a high fructose diet), they support our observations that the Mondo pathway plays an important role in the regulation of cholesterol/steroid metabolism also under non-disease conditions.
evidence: Inference based on comparison with literature

claim: Nonsense mediated decay products of the mutated transcript are proposed to trigger transcriptional upregulation of homologous genes that compensate for the mutant gene's function.
source: Nonsense mediated decay products of the mutated transcript are proposed to trigger transcriptional upregulation of homologous genes that compensate for the mutant gene's function (El-Brolosy et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to El-Brolosy et al., 2019

claim: Concerted changes across the entire cholesterol/steroid biosynthesis pathway are needed to rescue epiboly progression in the absence of MondoA function.
source: Apparently, concerted changes across the entire cholesterol/steroid biosynthesis pathway are needed to rescue epiboly progression in the absence of MondoA function.
evidence: Inference based on gene expression analysis

claim: Random variation in the amount of material deposited by the mother or in protein expression of key genes may limit compensation in the MZmondoa mutants with affected epiboly.
source: Furthermore, random variation in the amount of material deposited by the mother or in protein expression of key genes may limit compensation in the mutants with affected epiboly.
evidence: Speculation about mechanisms

claim: Incomplete penetrance is a frequent phenomenon in human genetic diseases and has been attributed to a wealth of mechanisms, which have been suggested as targets for therapy.
source: Importantly, incomplete penetrance is a frequent phenomenon in human genetic diseases and has been attributed to a wealth of mechanisms, which have been suggested as targets for therapy (Cooper et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cooper et al., 2013

claim: Future studies on how disturbed MondoA function is buffered during development might open leads to manipulating dysregulated Mondo pathway function in adult metabolic regulation.
source: Future studies how disturbed MondoA function is buffered during development might open leads to manipulating dysregulated Mondo pathway function in adult metabolic regulation.
evidence: Speculation about future research directions

claim: Steroidogenic enzymes are expressed in extraembryonic tissues in both fish and mice.
source: For example, steroidogenic enzymes are expressed in extraembryonic tissues in both fish and mice, the fish YSL (Hsu et al., 2006; Hsu et al., 2009) and the giant trophoblast cells of the murine placenta (Arensburg et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hsu et al., 2006; Hsu et al., 2009; Arensburg et al., 1999

claim: Zebrafish epiboly is analogous to the spreading of the trophectoderm during implantation.
source: Indeed, it has been proposed that zebrafish epiboly is analogous to the spreading of the trophectoderm during implantation (Kane and Adams, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kane and Adams, 2002

claim: Epiboly movements are severely impaired upon knockdown of the zebrafish homolog of solute carrier family 3 member 2 (Slc3a2).
source: Consistent with this idea, epiboly movements are severely impaired upon knockdown of the zebrafish homolog of solute carrier family 3 member 2 (Slc3a2) (Takesono et al., 2012), a factor crucial for trophoblast cell adhesion, migration and fusion in mammals (Kabir-Salmani et al., 2008; Kudo et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Takesono et al., 2012

claim: Slc3a2 is a factor crucial for trophoblast cell adhesion, migration and fusion in mammals.
source: Consistent with this idea, epiboly movements are severely impaired upon knockdown of the zebrafish homolog of solute carrier family 3 member 2 (Slc3a2) (Takesono et al., 2012), a factor crucial for trophoblast cell adhesion, migration and fusion in mammals (Kabir-Salmani et al., 2008; Kudo et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kabir-Salmani et al., 2008; Kudo et al., 2003

claim: It is conceivable that developmental functions of MondoA are conserved among vertebrates.
source: Thus, it is conceivable that developmental functions of MondoA are conserved among vertebrates.
evidence: Speculation based on comparative observations

claim: Mutations in the NSDHL gene in humans have been linked to an X-linked dominant condition called CHILD syndrome.
source: Importantly, mutations in the NSDHL gene in humans have been linked to an X-linked dominant condition called CHILD syndrome ('congenital hemidysplasia with ichthyosiform erythroderma and limb defects', reviewed in Herman, 2000) that is usually lethal in males (Bornholdt et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Herman, 2000 and Bornholdt et al., 2005

claim: CHILD syndrome is usually lethal in males.
source: Importantly, mutations in the NSDHL gene in humans have been linked to an X-linked dominant condition called CHILD syndrome ('congenital hemidysplasia with ichthyosiform erythroderma and limb defects', reviewed in Herman, 2000) that is usually lethal in males (Bornholdt et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bornholdt et al., 2005

claim: Murine male embryos carrying Nsdhl mutations die shortly after implantation.
source: Murine male embryos carrying Nsdhl mutations die shortly after implantation, and those carrying moderate or mild alleles showed reduced placental thickness with a poorly vascularized fetal labyrinth (Caldas et al., 2005; Liu et al., 1999 and references therein).
evidence: Supported by citations to Caldas et al., 2005; Liu et al., 1999

claim: Murine male embryos carrying moderate or mild Nsdhl alleles showed reduced placental thickness with a poorly vascularized fetal labyrinth.
source: Murine male embryos carrying Nsdhl mutations die shortly after implantation, and those carrying moderate or mild alleles showed reduced placental thickness with a poorly vascularized fetal labyrinth (Caldas et al., 2005; Liu et al., 1999 and references therein).
evidence: Supported by citations to Caldas et al., 2005; Liu et al., 1999

claim: In female mouse embryos carrying a maternal null Nsdhl allele, placental area was severely reduced.
source: Interestingly, also in female mouse embryos carrying a maternal null allele placental area was severely reduced (Cunningham et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cunningham et al., 2010

claim: Paternal X chromosome inactivation in yolk sac endoderm and trophoblast-derived lineages causes complete loss of Nsdhl function only in these tissues in female mouse embryos carrying a maternal null allele.
source: In these embryos, paternal X chromosome inactivation in yolk sac endoderm and trophoblast-derived lineages causes complete loss of function only in these tissues.
evidence: Direct statement based on known biology

claim: Nsdhl may contribute to the development of the mammalian placenta by regulating microtubule stability.
source: Given the potential analogous functions of placenta and YSL (Carvalho and Heisenberg, 2010), our results regarding Nsdhl function in epiboly make it tempting to speculate that Nsdhl contributes to the development of the mammalian placenta by regulating microtubule stability.
evidence: Speculation based on study findings and literature

claim: Stability of microtubules plays a role in trophoblast differentiation and implantation based on in vitro studies.
source: Remarkably, stability of microtubules apparently plays a role in trophoblast differentiation and implantation based on in vitro studies (Bates and Kidder, 1984; Douglas and King, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bates and Kidder, 1984; Douglas and King, 1993
